style_guide.voice: lowercase casual, no periods at end of posts, storytelling structure (hook → tension → insight → takeaway), specific numbers and data, asks questions to drive replies, no emojis, no em dashes, founder voice with 20+ years paid media experience, pro-agency, demand-focused, 200-400 chars minimum per post
style_guide.avoid: corporate speak, AI-powered, emojis, em dashes, one-liners under 150 chars, listicle-style bullet dumps, product feature lists, engagement bait
style_guide.positioning: synter helps agencies and media buyers drive real demand by handling execution so they can focus on growth strategy. joel has 20+ years in paid media and built synter because he lived the problem

week_1.text:
unpopular opinion: the reason most paid media hires fail in 90 days isn't the person

it's that the company expected one human to manage google, meta, linkedin, analytics, landing pages, tracking, reporting, and strategy

that's not a job description, that's a burnout prescription

i've watched this play out dozens of times over 20 years. the hire isn't bad. the expectations are impossible

we analyzed our own google ads account last week and found something wild

desktop converts at 2.4x better CPA than mobile on search

but mobile was eating 61% of spend because we left device bids on auto

one GAQL query, one bid modifier change, instant 18% CPA improvement

how many accounts are bleeding money on mobile right now because nobody ran the query

broke our reddit ads integration three times this week

turns out reddit's oauth endpoint silently drops your refresh_token when PKCE code_challenge is present. no error, no warning. your connection just dies after 60 minutes

took 3 days to diagnose, 4 lines to fix

building ad platform integrations is 20% feature work and 80% reading undocumented API behavior in discord threads from 2023

pulled similarweb on 5 competitors in our space last month

every single one had less than 1% of traffic from paid search. wide open channel

but here's what was interesting: 3 of them were getting 1600+ visits/mo from chatgpt and perplexity

we were getting zero

LLM visibility is the new SEO and almost nobody is tracking it yet. if AI agents recommend your competitor and not you, you lose before the click even happens

every ad platform is shipping AI campaign creation this year

none of them will manage the other platform's campaigns

google's AI won't optimize your meta spend. meta's AI won't touch your linkedin budget. and no platform has any incentive to tell you to shift budget away from them

cross-platform is the moat nobody's building because every platform wants to be the only platform

that's the gap

the search term audit we ran yesterday found $340/week in wasted spend

someone was searching "googleads doubleclick net" and clicking our ad. another was searching "free google ads course"

both had 50+ clicks over the past month

nobody checks search terms weekly because it takes 20 minutes per campaign across platforms. but the math is simple: $340/week × 52 weeks = $17,680/year in garbage clicks

what's your search term hygiene actually look like

shipped the campaign IDE this week and learned something about how media buyers actually want to work

they don't want a chat interface that does magic behind a curtain. they want to see the campaign structure, edit it inline, approve each step

the chat-first AI hype got this wrong. experienced media buyers want control with speed, not autopilot

so we built a hybrid: conversational creation, visual editing, one-click launch. the IDE metaphor from software engineering actually maps perfectly to campaign management

genuine question for agency media buyers

what percentage of your week is actually spent on strategy vs execution

i keep hearing 20/80 (20% strategy, 80% execution) and every single person says it should be the opposite

if that's true for you, what's the one execution task you'd eliminate first

the worst advice in B2B marketing right now is "just run linkedin ads"

nobody tells you linkedin's minimum viable test is $3k/mo because CPMs are $80-120. nobody mentions that lead gen forms have a 40% fake-email rate. nobody warns you that the audience targeting UI has 47 clicks before you can launch

linkedin ads work incredibly well for the right ICP at the right budget. but the "just run linkedin" crowd is setting people up to waste their first $5k and conclude the platform doesn't work

here's a cross-platform signal most people miss because they never see all their data in one place

when linkedin CPL drops 22% and google CPA rises 15% on the same audience segment in the same week

that's not random noise. that's your audience shifting channels. the correct move is to reallocate budget toward linkedin for that segment immediately

but if you're logging into each platform separately and comparing in a spreadsheet on friday, you're 5 days late

real-time cross-platform visibility isn't a nice-to-have. it's the difference between reactive and proactive

we just got our MCP server working with claude, cursor, and amp simultaneously

what this means in practice: a developer can ask claude to pull google ads performance, pause underperforming campaigns, reallocate budget to meta, and generate fresh creative — all from one terminal session

the MCP distribution insight that keeps me up at night: when someone asks an AI agent to "create a google ads campaign," the agent routes to whichever MCP server can execute it. the user never sees alternatives

first-mover in MCP = default tool for every AI agent. that's not a feature, it's a distribution channel

what's the most expensive mistake you've made in paid media that wasn't a strategy mistake

i'm talking wrong geo targeting, forgotten campaign pause over a weekend, budget set to daily instead of lifetime

mine was $2k on a test campaign i forgot to pause before a holiday weekend. classic

these execution errors cost more than bad strategy and nobody tracks them

hot take after 20 years in paid media: the agencies that win in 2026 won't be the ones with the most people

they'll be the ones whose people spend the most time on strategy

i've seen 3-person agencies outperform 30-person agencies because the small team had zero execution overhead. every hour went to thinking, testing, iterating

the big agency had 25 people in dashboards and 5 people thinking. the math doesn't work no matter how many people you hire

the landing page data keeps proving the same thing

homepage as landing page: 75% bounce rate, $47 CPA
dedicated LP matched to keyword: 35% bounce rate, $19 CPA

that's a 2.5x CPA improvement from one change

but most teams don't build dedicated LPs because it requires a designer, a developer, tracking pixel setup, and 2 weeks of back-and-forth

we got this down to 90 seconds: describe the page → generate → auto-inject all tracking pixels → host instantly

the bottleneck was never the ad. it was always the page the ad points to

ran a competitive analysis on 12 AI ad tools this week

9 of them position as "AI-powered optimization" — meaning they read your data and suggest changes you still have to make manually

2 of them can create campaigns on one platform

none of them handle the full loop across multiple platforms: research → create → launch → track → optimize → report

the market is flooded with copilots. nobody's building the execution layer

that's why we're building synter as an agent, not an assistant

if adding a new ad platform to your mix added zero workload — no new dashboard, no new learning curve, no new reporting format

which platform would you test first

most people say tiktok or reddit. cheapest CPMs, untapped B2B audiences, but "we don't have bandwidth for another dashboard"

that's not a strategy problem. that's a tooling problem

friday build update from synter

this week we shipped:
→ imagen 4 creative generation directly in campaign creation flow
→ negative keyword audit that runs across all campaigns in one command
→ CRM audience sync from attio/hubspot to 10 ad platforms simultaneously
→ device bid adjustments based on conversion data pulled via GAQL

the creative gen one is my favorite. describe what you want, get 4 variations, pick one, it's attached to your campaign. no canva, no designer queue, no waiting

we used to spend 3 hours per client on creative production. now it's 3 minutes

the pricing model for ad tools is broken and nobody wants to say it

most tools charge percentage of ad spend. so a tool that saves you $10k/month in wasted spend is incentivized to... not save you that money

we charge $49/month flat. same price whether you manage $5k or $500k in ad spend

aligned incentives matter. if your tool makes more money when you spend more, ask yourself who it's really optimized for

the CRM retargeting play most agencies skip because it's too much manual work:

→ sync closed-lost deals to google customer match
→ run search ads on competitor keywords to just that list
→ they already know you, now they see you everywhere they search

conversion rates on this audience are 3-5x higher than cold search

but nobody does it because syncing CRM lists to ad platforms means CSV exports, email hashing, manual uploads, and refreshing weekly

we automated the entire thing into one command. that's the kind of problem worth solving

end of week reflection: we're 6 months into building synter and the hardest part isn't the AI or the ad platform APIs

it's the 10,000 edge cases

google ads requires exact match on currency codes. meta silently rejects creatives over 125 chars in primary text on certain placements. linkedin's API returns different facet URNs depending on which endpoint you call

every integration is 20% building the feature and 80% handling the exceptions nobody documented

but every edge case we handle is one less thing a media buyer has to debug at 11pm

building cross-platform budget allocation on a saturday because the math is genuinely harder than the engineering

how do you compare a $12 linkedin CPL against a $3 google CPC against a $0.80 reddit CPM when each platform measures success differently

the answer is unified conversion tracking + attribution modeling + a lot of normalization

but when it works? rebalance $50k across 5 platforms in one sentence

that's worth a saturday

sunday question for the paid media folks

what's the one thing you wish your tools did that none of them do

for me it was always: show me all my campaigns across all platforms in one view and let me act on them without switching tabs

seems obvious. nobody built it. so we are

week_2.text:
the listicle SEO play is the most underrated distribution channel in B2B and it costs zero ad spend

google "best AI ad tools" — there are 47 articles ranking for buying-intent keywords. your competitor is in most of them. you're in none

each article sends traffic for years. each reader is actively evaluating tools

we got 3 placements in 2 weeks by emailing editors. total cost: $0. total time: 4 hours

meanwhile everyone's spending $15/click on the same keywords these articles rank for organically

we tracked conversion paths across platforms for 30 days and found something counterintuitive

the leads that converted fastest weren't the ones who clicked a google ad first. they were the ones who saw a linkedin ad, then searched our brand name on google, then converted

linkedin created awareness. google captured intent. attribution gave google 100% of the credit

if you're making budget decisions based on last-click attribution in 2026, you're probably cutting the channel that's actually driving your pipeline

cross-platform visibility isn't optional anymore

honest update: we rebuilt our campaign creation flow from scratch this week

the old flow was too linear — you had to go through 8 steps in order. felt like filling out a form

new flow lets you start anywhere. say "launch a search campaign for marketing automation keywords" and the agent fills in everything it can infer, shows you what it assumed, lets you override anything

the insight: AI campaign creation shouldn't feel like a wizard. it should feel like briefing a smart junior media buyer who already knows your account

interesting pattern from analyzing 50 SaaS companies' ad strategies this month

companies spending $50k+/mo on google ads almost always have one thing in common: dedicated landing pages per keyword cluster

companies spending under $10k almost always send traffic to their homepage

it's not that big spenders can afford better pages. it's that better pages made them confident enough to spend more

the LP is the unlock, not the budget

controversial: most "AI ad tools" are just GPT wrappers that generate ad copy and call it a day

generating headlines is maybe 2% of the work of running paid media

the other 98% is: keyword research, audience building, bid strategy, tracking setup, GTM configuration, conversion actions, negative keywords, device optimization, geo targeting, budget allocation, reporting, and actually pushing buttons in the platform

if your AI tool can write a headline but can't launch a campaign, it's a copywriter, not a media buyer

the competitor conquesting data is fascinating

we added exact match keywords for 4 competitor names: gomarble, ryze, albert, graphed

CPA on competitor keywords: $8.40
CPA on generic keywords: $34.20

4x better conversion rate because someone searching "[competitor name] alternative" already knows they need what you sell

but most companies don't run competitor campaigns because "it feels aggressive"

your competitors are bidding on your name right now. check your auction insights

the $49/month pricing decision was the scariest one we've made

every advisor said charge percentage of ad spend. "that's how the industry works." "you're leaving money on the table."

but percentage-of-spend pricing creates a perverse incentive: your tool makes more money when the client spends more, not when the client gets better results

flat pricing means we win when you win. we're incentivized to help you spend less on garbage and more on what converts

6 months in, no regrets. the trust it builds is worth more than the revenue we left behind

real talk: how many ad platforms does your team actually manage well vs how many do you have accounts on

most agencies I talk to have 5-6 platform accounts but really only optimize 2-3 consistently

the others get set-and-forget treatment. campaigns running on auto-bid with no search term audits for months

is that a team problem or a tooling problem

the conversion tracking crisis nobody talks about

we audited 15 google ads accounts last month. 11 of them had broken or misconfigured conversion tracking

missing GTM tags. unpublished containers. CAPI not connected. conversion windows set to 1 day instead of 30

these aren't small accounts. these are companies spending $20k+/month on ads with no idea which clicks actually convert

conversion tracking setup is 90% of campaign success. the other 10% is everything else combined

when we set up campaigns, tracking configuration is automatic. not optional, not a separate step, not something you can forget

ran an experiment: same offer, same audience definition, same budget, same creative concept across google, meta, linkedin, reddit, and tiktok

results after 14 days:
→ reddit: $4.20 CPL (lowest cost, highest intent)
→ google: $11.50 CPL (reliable, predictable)
→ meta: $8.30 CPL (best creative performance)
→ tiktok: $6.10 CPL (surprise performer for B2B)
→ linkedin: $38.00 CPL (highest quality leads)

if you're only on google and meta, you're leaving the cheapest leads on the table

but I get it — who has time for 5 dashboards

we made a mistake this month that taught us something important

we auto-enabled a campaign for a user without explicit approval. the campaign was configured correctly, budget was right, targeting was right

but the user wanted to review first. trust violated

new rule at synter: every campaign launches in PAUSED state. always. the human reviews, the human enables

AI agents should be fast, not presumptuous. the media buyer makes the final call, period

we shipped the fix the same day

for the agency owners: what would you do with 15 extra hours per week per media buyer

hire fewer people? take on more clients? spend more time on creative strategy?

curious because the answer reveals whether the bottleneck is headcount or leverage

prediction: within 18 months, the primary way businesses buy ad tech won't be through google searches or G2 reviews

it'll be through AI agent recommendations

when a marketing director asks claude "set up our Q3 paid media campaigns," the agent will route to whichever execution tool it trusts. the user never compares alternatives

this is why we're investing so heavily in our MCP server. being the best landing page matters less when the AI picks the tool

the new SEO is AI agent compatibility

the negative keyword data is staggering

we pulled search terms across all our campaigns for the past 30 days

23% of clicks came from irrelevant search terms. twenty-three percent

"free ad tools" "google ads certification" "how to get a job in marketing"

these clicks cost real money. on a $10k/month account, that's $2,300/month in waste

automatic negative keyword audits should run weekly. nobody does it because it takes 20 minutes per campaign

we run it in one command across every campaign simultaneously. it pays for itself in the first hour

the creative generation breakthrough we had this week

we connected imagen 4 directly into the campaign creation flow. so when the agent builds your campaign, it also generates the creative — matched to the platform specs, the audience, the offer

but here's what surprised us: the AI-generated creative performed within 8% of professional designer creative on meta

not because AI design is better. because speed beats perfection. you can test 10 AI creative variations in the time it takes to brief a designer on one

the winning strategy isn't AI OR human creative. it's AI for velocity, human for your hero campaigns

what's the most underrated ad platform for B2B right now

I'll go first: reddit

$4-8 CPMs, highly engaged audiences, subreddit targeting is basically intent-based, and almost no competition because "reddit ads are weird"

the brands willing to figure out reddit's quirks are getting absurd ROI while everyone fights over linkedin's $80+ CPMs

weekly build update

this week at synter:
→ campaign IDE now supports inline editing of ad copy before launch
→ added tiktok events API for server-side conversion tracking
→ microsoft ads offline conversions integration
→ fixed a bug where linkedin facet URNs changed between targeting and reporting endpoints (undocumented, naturally)

the linkedin bug was my favorite. their API returns different identifiers for the same audience depending on which endpoint you call. took 2 days to figure out, had to read their java SDK source code to confirm

nobody said ad platform APIs would be fun

the agencies charging 15-20% of ad spend for management are going to have a very rough 2027

not because AI replaces them. because AI makes it obvious how much of that fee was execution, not strategy

when campaign creation takes 90 seconds instead of 4 hours, when reporting is one query instead of a half-day, when tracking setup is automatic instead of a billable deliverable

the value shifts entirely to strategy. and strategy should be priced on outcomes, not on a percentage of spend

the best agencies are already making this shift. the rest are pretending it's not coming

something I've noticed after 20 years: the companies that succeed with paid media aren't the ones with the biggest budgets

they're the ones with the fastest iteration cycles

test a landing page monday. read the data tuesday. adjust wednesday. scale thursday

vs: brief the agency monday. review mockup thursday. get the page built next week. launch in 2 weeks. read data in 3 weeks

the first company runs 12 tests in the time the second runs 1

speed of iteration is the only durable advantage in paid media

heading into the weekend with a question

what's one thing about paid media you wish someone had told you 5 years ago

mine: the creative matters 10x more than the targeting. I spent years optimizing audiences when the headline was the real lever all along

saturday morning thought while debugging our budget allocation algorithm

the hardest problem in cross-platform advertising isn't technical. it's philosophical

how do you compare a linkedin impression to a google click to a reddit engagement when each platform defines success differently

you can't just normalize to CPA because the customer journey is multi-touch. you can't just look at last-click because that ignores awareness. you can't just look at impressions because that ignores intent

we're building something that weights each platform's contribution based on where it sits in the funnel. still early, but the results are promising

if anyone's solved this elegantly I want to hear about it

the future of agencies isn't fewer people doing more work

it's the same people doing fundamentally different work

execution handled by agents. strategy, relationships, and creative vision handled by humans

that's not a threat to the industry. it's the upgrade the industry has needed for a decade

the agencies that embrace this will attract better talent, retain them longer, and deliver better results

the ones that fight it will wonder why their best people keep leaving for in-house roles
